pack.name: Psychology
pack.title: The Locked Room of the Mind
pack.blurb: Thinkers, disorders, emotions, famous experiments and the wiring behind them.

prompts.flavor: Down here, every fear has a name. Some of them have names longer than you would think possible.
prompts.rules: Any named phobia, by its -phobia name. Phobias coined as jokes don't count.

answers.lore: Also an old name for rabies, which makes swallowing so painful that its victims come to dread water.
Fear of the number 13. Many buildings still skip the 13th floor.
Fear of the sea, and of what lives far beneath it. Reasonable, under the circumstances.
Fear of ghosts.
Fear of depths. You are reading this a long way down.
Fear of the number 666. The name is nearly as frightening as the number.
Fear of being buried alive. In the 1800s you could buy a coffin with a bell to ring.
Fear of very large things. Best to stay away from the bottom of the sea.
A vague and terrible dread of everything, with no particular cause.
Fear of infinity, and of things that never end.
Fear of trains or rail travel. The word was coined in the 1870s, when the railway age was about fifty years old.
Fear of Greek terms or jargon. Most of this list would set it off.

traps.reason: Give it its proper name, ending in -phobia.
Which one?
Fear of peanut butter sticking to the roof of your mouth. Coined as a joke, so the deep won't have it.
Fear of long words. A joke, and a cruel one.
The fear that somewhere, a duck is watching you. A cartoonist's joke.
A joke word for the fear of palindromes. Read it backwards.
An adjective, and usually about molecules.
The Greek god of fear, and a moon of Mars. Not a phobia.
A Far Side joke about wolves, socks and a freshly waxed floor.

prompts.source: Copied from the daily question "phobias" on 28 November 2026.

prompts.text: Name a part of the human brain.
prompts.flavor: It weighs about three pounds and holds every thought you have ever had. Some of them were not your own.
prompts.rules: Any named part of the human brain: lobes, folds, nuclei, chambers and the membranes that wrap it. Single cells, and the nerves that leave it, don't count.

answers.lore: Latin for 'little brain'. Small as it is, it holds most of the brain's neurons.
Named after the seahorse, for its curled shape. In London cabbies it grows as they learn the city's streets.
About the size of an almond, it governs hunger, thirst, body heat and sleep.
From the Greek for 'almond', which it resembles in size and shape.
Named for its pine-cone shape. Descartes believed it was the principal seat of the soul.
A bridge of some 200 million nerve fibres joining the two halves of the brain.
Named after Paul Broca, whose patient of 1861 could say only one word: 'tan'.
Latin for 'island': a whole lobe hidden deep inside a fold of the brain.
Latin for 'black substance', for the dark pigment in its cells.
The body's master clock, perched just above where the optic nerves cross, so daylight can set it.
A ring of arteries beneath the brain, named after Thomas Willis, who described it in 1664.
The brain's vomiting centre. It sits outside the blood-brain barrier, so it can taste poisons in the blood.
Latin for 'tree of life': the white matter inside the cerebellum, which branches like a tree when cut.

answers.answer: Bed nucleus of the stria terminalis

answers.lore: Francis Crick was still revising a paper about it the day he died, in 2004. He suspected it might conduct consciousness.
Latin for 'blue spot', and it really is bluish. It floods the brain with noradrenaline when alarm strikes.
Latin for 'uncertain zone'. Auguste Forel named it in 1877, saying nothing certain could be said about it.

traps.reason: The whole thing. The deep wants a piece of it.
The brain has several lobes. Name one.
The brain has hundreds of nuclei. Name one.
Joined to the brain at its base, but not part of it.
The bone around the brain, not part of it.
A single cell. The brain has some 86 billion of them.
A junction between two cells, far too small to count as a part.
Strictly an outgrowth of the brain, but it counts as a nerve, and nerves are left out.
A nerve leaving the brain, not part of it.
The fluid the brain floats in, not a part of it.
What the brain does, not a part of it.
Freud's parts of the mind, not of the brain.
Not a part of the brain, whatever Descartes thought.
A discredited 1960s theory, not a real part of the brain.
Electrical rhythms, not a part of the brain.
A computer's idea of a brain, not a part of yours.
Part of a single nerve cell, far too small to count as a part of the brain.
A chemical messenger, not a part of the brain.
A single kind of cell, far too small to count as a part.
Grown out of the brain before birth, but it belongs to the eye now.
That's the whole brain. Which part?

prompts.source: Copied from the daily question "brain-parts" on 28 November 2026.

prompts.text: Name a famous psychologist or psychiatrist.
prompts.flavor: They spent their lives watching other people think. It did some of them no good at all.
prompts.rules: Anyone famous for studying the mind or behaviour. Surnames are fine.

answers.lore: A Melbourne psychiatrist who, in 1949, found that lithium calmed mania, working in a disused hospital kitchen and testing the dose on himself first.
Adelaide-born, he ran the 1920s Hawthorne studies in Chicago, which found that factory workers did better simply because someone was paying attention to them.
A Bardi woman from the Kimberley, and the first Aboriginal psychologist to graduate in Australia.

traps.reason: A great thinker about people, but not remembered as a psychologist.
Name a real one, by name.

prompts.text: Name a mental health condition or psychological disorder.
prompts.flavor: The mind can turn on itself in more ways than there are names for. These are the names.
prompts.rules: Any recognised mental, neurodevelopmental or behavioural condition, by its clinical or common name.

answers.lore: The fixed belief that you are dead, do not exist, or have lost your organs. Described in 1880 by Jules Cotard, whose patient saw no need to eat.
A sudden terror that one's genitals are shrinking into the body and that death will follow. It comes in epidemics: Singapore had hundreds of cases in 1967.

traps.reason: Part of being human, and sometimes very hard, but not a diagnosis in itself.
A condition of the brain and nerves, treated by a neurologist rather than counted as a mental disorder.
Which one? Name the condition.

prompts.flavor: You have felt all of these. One of them you are feeling now, and would rather not say.
prompts.rules: Any feeling or mood a person can have, including words borrowed from other languages.

answers.lore: The Baining people of Papua New Guinea name the heaviness left behind when guests depart. They leave a bowl of water out overnight to soak it up.
An Inuit word for the fidgety anticipation of waiting for a visitor, which sends you outside again and again to see if they are coming.
"The call of the void": the sudden, unwanted urge to jump when standing on a high place. Researchers find it is common, and not a wish to die.

traps.reason: A sensation in the body rather than an emotion.
Which one? Name it.

prompts.text: Name a famous psychology experiment or study.
prompts.flavor: Somebody volunteered. Somebody signed a form. Nobody told them what was really being measured.
prompts.rules: Any well-known experiment, study or case in psychology, by its usual name or by the researcher's.

aliases: On being sane in insane places

answers.lore: In 1939 Iowa researchers told orphans with normal speech that they stuttered, to see if it would make them. For some it did, for life.
A horse in 1900s Berlin that appeared to do arithmetic by tapping a hoof. He was really reading his questioner's face. Researchers have feared the effect ever since.
In 1959 Milton Rokeach brought together three patients who each believed he was Jesus, to see whose belief would give way. None did. He later apologised.

traps.reason: An experiment, real or imagined, but from another field.
Which one? Name it.

prompts.text: Name a type of therapy or psychological treatment.
prompts.flavor: Lie back. Tell me about the first thing you remember. No, the one before that.
prompts.rules: Any talking therapy, behavioural technique, medication class or other treatment for the mind.

answers.lore: A Japanese treatment from 1919 that begins with a week of total bed rest and silence. You are asked to accept your feelings, not to fix them.
At Sydney's Chelmsford Private Hospital in the 1960s and 70s, patients were kept in a drugged coma for weeks. At least 24 died. A royal commission followed.
Erasmus Darwin's idea, taken up by Benjamin Rush: strap the patient into a chair and spin it until the madness, or the patient, gave out.

traps.reason: A treatment, but for the body rather than the mind.
Which treatment? Name it.

prompts.text: Name a defence mechanism or a cognitive bias.
prompts.flavor: The mind lies to itself all day, kindly and expertly. It is doing it now.
prompts.rules: Any way the mind protects itself from discomfort, or any systematic error in how people think and judge.

answers.lore: Believing that a vague description, true of nearly anyone, was written just for you. It is how horoscopes work.
Rejecting new evidence because it contradicts what everyone knows. Named for the doctor who showed in 1847 that washing hands saved mothers, and was ignored.
A family drives 85 kilometres through Texas heat to a dinner none of them wanted, each going along because they thought the others were keen. Named in 1974.

traps.reason: A behaviour, perhaps a telling one, but not a named mechanism or bias.
Which one? Name it.

prompts.text: Name a branch of psychology or a school of thought within it.
prompts.flavor: A hundred and fifty years of argument about what a mind is. Nobody has won yet.
prompts.rules: Any field, specialty, approach or perspective in psychology.

answers.lore: Reading character from the bumps of the skull. It was nonsense, but its core idea, that different parts of the brain do different jobs, turned out to be right.
The study of the hidden motives behind historical events, often by putting dead leaders on the couch. Isaac Asimov borrowed the word for predicting the future.
William McDougall's theory that all behaviour is driven by purpose and instinct. From the Greek hormē, an urge. It lost to behaviourism and is all but forgotten.

traps.reason: A neighbour of psychology, or a pretender, but not a branch of it.
Which branch? Name it.
